newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Cyprus leaders begin talks with modest expectations.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus leaders begin talks with modest expectations.

text.p: The leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities meet on Wednesday with only modest hopes of reviving negotiations aimed at ending the partition of their island by establishing a federal system.

The encounter, at a rural retreat called Troutbeck, 90 miles (145 kms) north of New York City, is the first face-to-face meeting in nearly three years between President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.
Secretary-General Kofi Annan opens the talks, due to last until Sunday and likely to be followed by another round next month near Geneva.
An election campaign in the Greek Cypriot south of the island is expected to put a damper on further negotiations until after next February's presidential vote.

Clerides, who is still considering whether to run for re-election, told Reuters the meetings provide an opportunity to "exchange views on some of the main issues, perhaps agree on an agenda for the next talks, and measure how flexible the other side is."

Denktash said this round should be confined to taking "soundings," adding: "If sounding results in some sort of mutual understanding on some of the issues, then I think we shall have a chance of going to the second round."
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since troops from Turkey took over the north of the island in 1974 in reaction to a coup in Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.

But the Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government including representatives of both communities broke apart amid violence that prompted the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force.
It still patrols a buffer zone stretching 112 miles (180 km) across the island, where some 30,000 Turkish troops are still stationed and the Nicosia government has been beefing up its armament.

The Greek Cypriot-led administration is regarded internationally as the legitimate government of the whole of Cyprus. Only Ankara recognises a Turkish Cypriot state established in 1983 with Denktash as president.

The negotiations mark the latest U.N. attempt over more than two decades to reunite the island as a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation and end a major source of friction between Greece and Turkey, historic antagonists despite their membership in NATO.

The Greek Cypriots, comprising about 80 percent of the island's population of fewer than 800,000, envision a solution based on the devolution of power, granting each community a degree of autonomy while retaining as many elements as possible of a strong central government.
The Turkish Cypriots see a federation as arising through the surrender of some powers by two independent sovereign entities.

Each side's vision contains elements that are anathema to the other, such as the Greek Cypriot wish for freedom of settlement and the right to own property anywhere in the island, and the Turkish Cypriot insistence on the sovereign equality of each community.

After delivering an opening speech, Annan hands over to his special adviser for Cyprus, former Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez, who has 25 years' experience as a U.N. official. As an under-secretary-general, he helped negotiate the 1988 Geneva accords that led to the departure of Soviet troops from Afghanistan.
Two looming events have added urgency to efforts at least to get the diplomatic ball rolling.
Talks expected to begin next year on European Union membership for Cyprus would be much smoother if an end to the island's division were at least in sight.

Another spur is the Nicosia government's planned deployment in 1998 of Russian-made S-300 ground defence missiles. Turkey, with air bases little more than 40 miles (65 km) away, fears they could deny it air superiority and has vowed to use any means to block installation of the missiles.

Most of the participants in the talks, as well as special envoys appointed by a number of countries to keep watch on Cyprus developments, attended a dinner Tuesday night at Annan's New York residence.
